Reach the agent from anywhere, and answer the app question honestly

An app cannot put your carrier number on the agent, and no amount of
Kotlin changes that: inbound calls to a mobile number are delivered by the
carrier's IMS to the SIM that owns it, authenticated with keys inside the
SIM. No application can register for that. So there are two paths, and
both now exist:

  * data (free, no telephone company): your phone opens a socket to the
    agent. This is `phone voice web` plus the Android client in android/.
  * PSTN (a rented DID, ~$1-3/mo): your carrier number genuinely rings, the
    carrier bridges into your Asterisk, and the agent answers - the block
    to add is written out in voice/trunk.conf.example.

`phone voice web` serves a self-contained browser client (no CDN, no
framework - a client that phones home would defeat the point), an RFC 6455
WebSocket audio bridge implemented in the standard library, and a small
JSON API: ring my phone, leave a note, ask a question, read the last
transcript. It reuses the phone line's CallSession, so the VAD, whisper,
Ollama, barge-in and transcripts are the same code, and the browser gets
live turn events over the same socket.

The Android client speaks that protocol with the pieces a browser cannot
provide: VOICE_COMMUNICATION capture (the platform echo canceller, without
which the agent hears itself), a foreground service so a call survives the
screen going off, and ws:// inside a VPN - a browser refuses the microphone
over plain HTTP, an app does not. It is not built here (no Android SDK in
this environment) and android/README.md says so plainly.

Also in this commit:

  * [web] config section, refuse-by-default: a non-loopback bind needs
    allow_remote *and* a token, because this carries live audio and a
    dialling API. docs/REMOTE.md is the deployment story.
  * `phone voice note` and /api/note, so a remote client can brief the
    agent for the next call ("I am driving, keep it short").
  * /api/call-me validates through validate_dial_request exactly like the
    model's intent path: 911 and any non-owner number are refused before a
    dialler is reached, and a test asserts the request body cannot choose
    the number.
  * `phone status` probes ports instead of grepping for a process, because
    pgrep -f matches the caller's own command line (it reported a server
    that was not running), and `py -c` in the launcher never worked - the
    helper runs modules.

Bugs found while building the remote path:

  * a hangup discarded the audio already queued in front of it, so the last
    thing a caller said was thrown away - the normal shape of a call ending;
  * transcripts were silently skipped when their directory did not exist,
    which is exactly the first call a user wants to read.

435 assertions pass (308 pytest + 60 SIP + 45 firewall + 22 e2e).

Co-authored-by: arena-agent <297053741+arena-agent@users.noreply.github.com>

Put a local Ollama model on the phone line

Adds the voice agent: a local model that can answer a call and dial out,
bridged from Asterisk over AudioSocket. Standard library only for the
protocol, the audio maths, the Asterisk config generator, and the Ollama
client; whisper, Ollama, and Piper are optional adapters that fail with a
sentence rather than a traceback.

The dialling rule is the part that matters. Speech is untrusted input, so
the model is never shown the owner's number, may only propose
[[dial:owner]], and validate_dial_request() allows exactly the configured
destination. Emergency and service numbers are refused before that
comparison (the previous regex never matched 911 - the call was only
refused by coincidence), the config loader refuses to accept one as the
owner, and the generated dialplan contains the number literally with no
pattern that reaches the PSTN. `phone voice dial-test` proves it.

Bugs found and fixed while building this:

* the streaming resampler dropped the last sample of every chunk, so
  chunked audio was not the same signal as one-shot audio (clicks at every
  boundary and roughly twice the perceived energy);
* playback was unpaced, so a reply was flushed into the socket faster than
  real time and Asterisk queued it - latency that grows every turn;
* a peer closing the TCP connection was invisible: a dropped call waited
  out the whole silence timeout on a dead line;
* a lone tone registered as a DTMF digit (the detector needed both the row
  and column tones, and its threshold was off by orders of magnitude);
* pcm16_from_float mapped -1.0 to -32767 instead of -32768;
* recv_audio returned "no audio" when it had actually received a keypress,
  and the offline WAV driver wrote its stand-in into ~/voice whether or
  not that directory existed;
* the Asterisk generator pointed at certificate filenames the rest of the
  project never generates, used an identify section matching 0.0.0.0/0
  (that identifies the whole internet as your handset), and put two allow=
  lines where one comma-separated line was meant.

Also: `phone voice` is now the agent (the pjsua launcher keeps `phone sip`),
`phone doctor`/`phone status` report it, both installers copy voice/, and
docs/VOICE.md answers the VoLTE question directly: a server cannot hold
VoLTE, so a real mobile number means a rented DID and an ordinary bridged
call - the model half is free, the PSTN half is not.

386 assertions pass (259 pytest + 60 SIP + 45 firewall + 22 e2e).

Co-authored-by: arena-agent <297053741+arena-agent@users.noreply.github.com>

Tie the three legs together, and fix the bugs that joining them exposed

Nothing here can buy a DID, reach into a LAN, or receive a provider's webhook;
that is stated plainly in the README rather than implied. What this adds is the
tooling that makes each leg verifiable one at a time, plus the fixes that only
showed up once the legs were wired together.

New:
  sip/test-tls.sh     DNS, TCP, TLS handshake, certificate verification, subject
                      and SANs, then an unauthenticated SIP OPTIONS probe - so a
                      registration failure can be attributed to the network, the
                      certificate, or the credentials instead of guessed at. It
                      also recognises a TLS-inspecting middlebox, which is the
                      failure mode that looks most like "wrong password".
  sip/provision.sh    writes the account block from a provider template,
                      expanding @HOME@, preferring the user's CA bundle,
                      generating a client certificate if absent, and quoting any
                      value containing '#' so pjsua's parser cannot truncate it.
  sip/providers/      telnyx, flowroute, twilio (marked unverified) and asterisk
                      blocks, each with the provider-side checklist.
  sip/phone.sh doctor audio hardware, group membership, ALSA devices, and
                      pjsua's own device indexes; runs before the config checks
                      so it answers "can this box hear me?" on a bare machine.
  sms/cli.py test     self-test of the whole local text path (real HTTP -> spool
                      -> read) that then prints the exact webhook URL, header
                      format and tunnel recipe for the provider.

Parser bugs found by reading pjsua's read_config_file(), each now regression
tested. All of these produced configs that looked right and would have failed
against a real provider:
  - "\;transport=tls" in URIs. pjsua does no backslash unescaping, so the
    backslash reached the URI parser and the transport parameter was misparsed.
    My own first template shipped this.
  - '#' ends a line anywhere, so a password containing it is silently
    truncated; unquoted '#' is now refused and provisioning quotes such values.
  - config lines are read into a 200-byte buffer; over-long lines are now
    rejected instead of silently truncated.

Integration bugs found by exercising the whole command path:
  - `phone sip doctor` (bare word, as documented) was treated as a call target
    and executed pjsua: a diagnostic that would place a call.
  - `phone sip provision --provider X` died in the option loop before reaching
    the delegate.
  - `phone sms test --spool-dir X` failed: global flags only parsed before the
    subcommand.
  - provision pointed at a client certificate it never generated.
  - `phone sip test-tls` reported "negotiated TLSv1.2" on a failed handshake,
    because openssl prints the protocol it attempted.
  - a bad spool path produced a Python traceback instead of a sentence.

Tests: 265 assertions (138 python, 60 sip, 45 firewall, 22 e2e), still needing
no root, no provider and no network. Voice remains the one leg that cannot be
verified from here - no sound card, no pjsua, and an egress proxy that
terminates TLS - which sip/test-tls.sh reports as exactly that.

Co-authored-by: arena-agent <297053741+arena-agent@users.noreply.github.com>

Add terminal-native voice + text stack with a default-deny firewall

Three components, one command line, no GUI, no mobile OS, no telemetry.

voice (sip/)
  pjsua.conf.example  TLS-only signalling, mandatory SRTP, explicit CA file,
                      DTLS-SRTP preferred, log level pinned so SDP (and thus
                      SDES key material) is never written to disk.
  phone.sh            verifies before it execs: pjsua must be built with TLS
                      and SRTP, the config and private key must be mode 0600,
                      placeholders filled, --use-tls/--no-udp/--no-tcp/
                      --use-srtp 2/--tls-ca-file/--tls-verify-server present,
                      log level <= 3, and srtp-secure=2 only with sips: URIs.
  gen-certs.sh        client certificate plus an explicit CA bundle, because
                      PJLIB's OpenSSL backend ignores the system trust store.

text (sms/)
  spool.py    one message per plain text file: atomic writes, 0600/0700,
              sanitised sender slug plus content-addressed filename, SHA256
              digest, metadata-only journal, arrival timestamp, size caps.
  daemon.py   stdlib HTTP webhook receiver: token auth (constant time), body
              cap, rate limit, content-type allowlist, replay suppression,
              loopback-only unless the operator explicitly opts in with
              token + TLS.
  poll.py     puller for gateways that cannot push, with a crash-safe cursor
              and retry-after-failure semantics.
  cli.py      list/read/tail/grep/stats/verify/export/purge. `tail --follow`
              watches filenames, which `tail -f ~/sms/incoming/*.txt` cannot.

firewall (lockdown.sh)
  Default deny in/out/forward. Every peer is pinned by resolved address; IPv6
  is dropped (a v4-only ruleset on a live v6 stack is a leak); DNS goes only to
  the named resolver; the SRTP window matches pjsua's real default (4000-4010).
  Rules are validated with nft --check and backed up before applying, and
  --panic-timeout arms a rollback so a remote shell is not a one-way trip.

Corrections to the original draft, documented in the README with reasons:
--with-srtp is not a pjproject option; --sip-border is not a pjsua option;
--local-port 5061 puts TLS on 5062 (pjsua binds local port + 1), so the config
uses 5060 -> 5061; --srtp-secure=2 requires sips: URIs; --tls-verify-server
needs --tls-ca-file; pjsua's default log level dumps SIP messages; the
`tail -f glob` recipe never sees later files; and the UFW sketch's
"allow out to any port 443/53" rules are exactly how telemetry survives a
"lockdown".

Tests: 132 Python + 35 SIP + 45 firewall + 22 end-to-end assertions
(./tests/run.sh), none needing root, a provider, or network access.

Co-authored-by: arena-agent <297053741+arena-agent@users.noreply.github.com>

Co-authored-by: arena-agent <297053741+arena-agent@users.noreply.github.com>

Atrium: gemma-avatar with eyes — real-time camera vision for local Ollama models

Atrium is gemma-avatar, complete and unchanged (silero-VAD → parakeet STT →
Ollama → Qwen3-TTS → TalkingHead 3D avatar over the OpenAI Realtime WS
protocol), plus the one thing it could not do: see the user back.

The voice pipeline is untouched. What is new is a second, independent input
that joins it at the Ollama step — a live webcam perception loop whose
observations are pushed into the same conversation.

Three perception layers, each of which degrades on its own:

  motion.js     frame differencing, zero dependencies, ~1ms/frame. Always on.
                Answers "are you there / did you move / which way".
  landmarks.js  MediaPipe hands/pose/face, optional (download_vision_assets.py).
                Exact finger counts, hand position, posture, lean, face.
  frames        JPEG stills sent as input_image for a vision-capable model.

Finger counting is the headline case and needs no vision model: a finger
counts as up when its tip is farther from the wrist than its middle knuckle
(distance test, so it survives rotation), the thumb against the pinky
knuckle. That makes it instant and correct on a text-only model.

Built for a slow machine on purpose. The loop (eyes.js) times each pass and
stretches its own interval to match — a 400ms pass becomes a ~600ms cadence
instead of a queue of frames. Every vision path is optional and wrapped: no
camera, no models, no GPU and no network each degrade to "still talking,
just not seeing".

Also:
  - /lab, a Camera Lab that runs the whole pipeline with no model attached,
    and prints the exact text Atrium hands the model.
  - five new model tools: look_at_camera, count_my_fingers,
    describe_what_you_see, start_watching_me, stop_watching_me.
  - server-side frame handling in local_s2s_launcher.py: camera frames and
    uploads are resized before they reach the model (a 1.5M-char frame drops
    to 80K), with ATRIUM_* knobs and ATRIUM_STRIP_IMAGES for text-only models.
  - wires up the avatar-parts panel that was dead markup upstream.
  - 23 tests for the pure vision logic (bun test).

Co-authored-by: arena-agent <297053741+arena-agent@users.noreply.github.com>
